text: Generalize what made the Steane code work, and you get the dominant family of practical quantum codes — including, as you'll see next chapter, the surface code itself.

A CSS code is built from a pair of classical linear codes, C1 and C2, satisfying one structural condition: the dual of C2 must be a subset of C1. Given that, X-type stabilizers come from C1's parity-check structure, and Z-type stabilizers come from C2's. That nested condition is exactly what's needed to guarantee every X-type stabilizer commutes with every Z-type stabilizer — the same commutation requirement every valid stabilizer code must satisfy.

The Steane code is the case where C1 equals C2, both the Hamming 7,4 code — and that code satisfies the condition using itself on both sides, which is exactly the self-orthogonality you verified in the previous lesson. That's why the Steane code could reuse the same 3 rows of H for both its X-type and Z-type stabilizers: C1 and C2 are literally the same code. In general, C1 and C2 don't have to match — you're free to pick two different classical codes, as long as the nesting condition holds, opening up a much larger design space.

CSS codes dominate practical quantum error correction for a concrete reason: they let you reuse well-understood classical coding theory twice — once to handle X errors through C1, once to handle Z errors through C2 — instead of inventing new quantum-specific machinery. Decades of classical results on distance, decoding, and performance carry over directly to each half of the problem. This is exactly the structure behind the surface code, next chapter's subject and the leading practical candidate for real fault-tolerant hardware: X-type plaquette stabilizers and Z-type vertex stabilizers, CSS-paired on a 2D lattice instead of the Steane code's 7-qubit block.
Next lesson is this chapter's problem-solving lab: verifying self-orthogonality on specific rows of H, and computing real syndromes for specific injected errors on the Steane code, by hand.
